description.cancellation_policy:
If your plans change and you will not be using all or part of your permit, please make that cancellation on recreation.gov right away so that space can be made available to other interested hikers. Recreation.gov will award partial refunds of participant charges for cancellations made on the website at least 1-month prior to the permit start date provided the permit has not yet been printed.

When Does Recreation.gov Release Cancelled Space? When individuals cancel their permits on Recreation.gov, the space is randomly made available for new reservations some time within 24 hours.
description.description:
CAMPGROUND AND TRAIL CLOSURES:

  • Before planning your hike, review our Key Hiking Messages page for current trail closures and water availability.

  • Rim-to-Rim hiking will not be possible from 11:59p.m. on 10/15/2026 through approx. February 2027 due to the partial closure of the North Kaibab Trail.

PERMITS:

When to apply: See "Important Dates" (two sections below) for when backcountry permits become available.

Minimum Age: Applicants must be 18 years or older to apply for a Backcountry Permit or to be the trip leader for a Backcountry Permit. 

When Permits are Required: Backcountry Permits are Required for backpacking or camping anywhere in the park (exceptions listed below).  

Lottery Applicants: Each individual can submit one application per lottery (i.e., one per month). Recreation.gov has taken precautions to limit users to 1 profile each. Grand Canyon will take additional steps to revoke permits from any individual who finds a way to submit multiple applications under their own name. Reservations revoked for this reason will not be eligible for a refund.

A Grand Canyon BACKCOUNTRY Permit is NOT Required for:

  • Car Campgrounds :

    • Overnight camping at Mather Campground , Trailer Village , or Desert View Campground 

    • Overnight camping at North Rim Campground closed

  • Phantom Ranch Lodge : 

    • Stays at Phantom Ranch Lodge 

  • Guided overnight hikes :

    • The Grand Canyon Conservancy Field Institute offers educational backpacking trips and obtains backcountry permits which cover all participants on their trips. Permits are issued in the Institute's name - participants do not need separate permits. Visit Grand Canyon Conservancy for more info.

    • Commercially guided backcountry hiking with companies who have been issued a Commercial Use Authorization and have obtained a backcountry permits. Permits are issued in the name of the company guiding the hike - participants do not need separate permits. Visit Guided Hikes. 

  • Day hikes :

    • Note: Any organized, non-commercial group of 12-30 participants, or not-for-profit group conducting rim-to-rim, rim-to-rim-to-rim, rim-to-river-to-rim, and/or extended day hikes in the inner canyon must obtain a Special Use Permit. 

  • Day stock rides (i.e. horse or mule rides)

    • concessioner mule rides (South Rim or North Rim)

    • riding your own horses or mules

  • Noncommercial River Trips : 

    • A Grand Canyon National Park noncommercial RIVER permit is required

Important Notes:

  • Pets : Pets are not allowed below the rim.

  • Service Animals : If you wish to hike below the rim with your service animal, please start by visiting the Backcountry Information Center and ask for information and advice to help make your trip safer both for you and for your service animal.

  • Access to Tribal Lands: Access to tribal land requires a permit from the respective tribe.

    • Havasupai Reservation 

    • Hualapai Nation 

    • Navajo Nation 

Recreation.gov: Recreation.gov has been used for all Grand Canyon Backcountry Permits since January 2024. Please see the park's Press Release Announcement and Frequently Asked Questions.
description.discounts: There are no discounts or discount passes that apply to Grand Canyon's Backcountry Permits.
description.driving_directions:
South Rim: The South Rim is open all year and located 60 miles (97 km) north of Williams, Arizona (via route 64 from Interstate 40) and 80 miles northwest of Flagstaff (via route 180). Grand Canyon lies entirely within the state of Arizona. 

North Rim: North Rim Roads and Services are closed for the Winter between December 1 and May 15. The North Rim is located 30 miles (48 km) south of Jacob Lake on Highway 67; the actual rim of the canyon is an additional 14 miles (23 km) south. Jacob Lake, AZ is located in northern Arizona on Highway 89A, not far from the Utah border.
description.fee_policy:
What are the Backcountry Permit Charges?

Basic Permit Charge: $10 (non-refundable). Waived for lottery winners and runners-up during the early access month when reserved through timeslot. 

Nightly Charge: (refundable until 30 days before permit start date provided permit has not yet been printed):

  • $15 per person or stock animal for below rim use.

  • $4 per person or stock animal for above rim use.

Permit holders are responsible for paying park entrance fees upon arrival.

When can the permit be printed?

Permits can be printed as early as one-month before the permit start date. Permittees can no longer directly modify or cancel their permits once printed - please reach out by email to a Ranger for assistance at grca_bic@nps.gov or 928-638-7875.

What happens if I forget to print my permit?

Stop by the Backcountry Information Center before your hike begins to acquire a printed permit.
description.lottery_information:
Grand Canyon uses a monthly lottery to ensure fair consideration of earliest requests for Backcountry Permits:

Lottery Applications: See "Important Dates" for the 2-week application periods.

Lottery Run: The lottery is run late on the 2nd of the month. It randomly reorders all applicants, giving the top 750 (in groups of 15) a date and time (a "timeslot") to log back in and make an actual itinerary reservation if space is available. There will be 5 timeslots per day (8am, 10am, noon, 2pm, and 4pm MST) over 10 days. For the current MST Time zone info, visit: Link.

Timeslot: When your timeslot comes up (or any time or day after within that lottery month), you can login to make up to 1 itinerary reservation if available. 

Applicants Not in the Top 750: Remaining lottery applicants can see and reserve any remaining space starting around the 20th of the month (see chart).

Open to All: After the lottery month is over, everyone can check availability and make reservations (if space is available).

Congratulations on securing a reservation for a backcountry permit! Here are a few reminders regarding your permit: 

Preparing: To help members of your group prepare and know what to expect on your hike, please have each of them read our Backcountry Hiking Brochure , visit our Hiking Tips page, watch the Grand Canyon Hiking Video , and review the backcountry rules and regulations . Additional helpful links are located at the bottom of this email.

Printing your Permit: We recommend waiting to print your permit until the week before your hike – once printed, Recreation.gov locks your reservation so it can no longer be modified or canceled without the help of a Ranger. Permits can be printed as early as 30-days before your start date. 

Canceling: If your plans change and you will not be using your reservation, please cancel on Recreation.gov as soon as possible so space can be freed up for other interested hikers. If you have already printed your permit and wish to cancel, Rangers are glad to help -- please send an email to grca_bic@nps.gov with your start date, reservation number, and ask for help canceling your permit.

Refunds: The deadline for refunds is 30-days prior to the permit start date. Cancellations made on Recreation.gov by this deadline will receive a refund of the nightly participant charges. The lottery/basic permit charge is not refundable. This 30-day deadline is designed to encourage cancellations far enough in advance for others across the country to be able to claim and use the space.

description.need_to_know_order:
The Trip Leader and/or participants can be cited for violating these regulations:

  • Permit Requirement: A Backcountry Permit is required for all overnight backcountry use and MUST be in your possession while in the Backcountry. The permit is valid only for the trip leader, campsites, dates, and number of people specified on the permit.

  • Campgrounds: Quiet hours are 8pm-6am. No smoking within 100' of campgrounds or 25' of Ranger Stations or Water Utility Buildings.

  • Trash: Carry out your trash. Burning, burying, or leaving trash or toilet paper is prohibited.

  • Affiliated Groups: Your permit is void if on any night another group affiliated to yours (i.e. same club, organization, family, group of friends, etc.) is using the same campground or use area. More than one group from the same organization or affiliation camping in the same designated campground or Use Area per night is prohibited.

  • Commercial Use: Commercial Use Authorization is required for Commercial Use of the backcountry.

  • Fires: Wood or charcoal fires of any type are prohibited. Sterno or fossil fuel backpack stoves are permitted.

  • Water: Use of biodegradable or any other type of soap in creeks or camping within 200' of any water source (except at designated sites) is prohibited.

  • Wildlife: Feeding, touching, teasing, or intentionally disturbing wildlife is prohibited.

  • Rocks: Throwing or rolling rocks or other items down hillsides or mountainsides, into valleys or canyons, or inside caves is prohibited.

  • Shortcutting: Leaving a trail or walkway to shortcut between portions of the same trail or walkway, or to shortcut to an adjacent trail is strictly prohibited.

  • Preservation: Possessing, destroying, injuring, defacing, removing, digging, or disturbing from its natural state any plants, rocks, animals, mineral, cultural or archeological resources, natural features, or signs is prohibited. Walking on, entering, traversing, or climbing on an archeological resource is prohibited.

description.need_to_know_permit:
DECIDE WHERE YOU WANT TO HIKE

Inner-Canyon Corridor

  • Bright Angel Campground is by far the most requested and highly popular below-rim backpacking destination within Grand Canyon National Park. Located near the confluence of Bright Angel Creek and the Colorado River, this campground has restrooms, potable water, shade trees, picnic tables, a Ranger Station, and proximity to the inner-canyon Phantom Ranch Lodge. This area is perfect for fit hikers who are ready for their first hike within the Grand Canyon backcountry.
  • The Bright Angel Trail and South Kaibab Trail both lead from the South Rim to Bright Angel Campground, and the North Kaibab Trail leads there from the North Rim. These three trails all connect at the bottom of the canyon over the Colorado River by way of two steady foot bridges. Because these are the only bridges within the entire Grand Canyon backcountry, this is called the "Trans-Canyon Corridor" or just "Corridor" (i.e. it is "the" way to get from one rim to the other). These trails are Grand Canyon's widest and best maintained inner-canyon trails.
  • Preferred Hike: Most choose to begin and end their hikes on the South Rim, and the most common backpacking itinerary they choose includes staying up to two-nights at Bright Angel Campground and/or up to two nights at Havasupai Gardens Campground. Backpackers hiking either direction between Bright Angel Campground and the North Rim (open mid-May through late November) should request to stay at Cottonwood Campground to split up the one-way 14.5 mile (23.3 km) hike which has a 6,000 feet (1,829 m) change in elevation.
  • See our Corridor Brochure for more information.

Hikes for Returning Grand Canyon Hikers

  • All hikes into and especially out of the canyon are difficult, and because of the difficulty most who hike the canyon only do so once. Nevertheless, some do return for at least a second hike. Many of these choose to do another hike in the Corridor or to branch out onto a harder, less commonly used trail.
  • The Hermit, Grandview, and Clear Creek trails are often recommended for second Grand Canyon hikes.
    • The Hermit Trail is a common choice for returning Grand Canyon hikers and is often recommended for a second backpacking trip in the canyon. However, many who hike here as their second Grand Canyon hike will rate the Hermit Trail as being twice as difficult. This may be due to mis-remembering the difficulty of their previous hike or simply due to the challenge of hiking on a steeper, narrower, looser treaded, and exposed trail. 
    • The Grandview Trail is another common choice for a second backpacking trip in the canyon. This trail descends to Horseshoe Mesa, an inner canyon plateau located about 2,500 feet (762 m) below the rim. Most who hike here seek to stay one or two nights then return to the rim.
    • The Clear Creek Trail starts at the bottom of the canyon by Bright Angel Campground and involves a 2 mile (3.2 km), 1,250 foot (381 m) climb before continuing another 7-miles (11.2 km) east to the Clear Creek drainage. Most who choose this hike seek a four night itinerary starting on the South Rim: first night at Bright Angel Campground, second and third nights in Clear Creek, and a fourth night back at Bright Angel Campground.

Advanced Hikes for Experienced GC Hikers

  • Grand Canyon National Park encompasses more than 1.2 million acres (4,856,228 ha), though much of the park is inaccessible due to the predominance of cliffs. Most of these areas are extremely remote and recommended only individuals who have extensive route finding ability and are highly experienced Grand Canyon hikers. The Colorado River bisects the canyon; there are bridges for hikers in the Phantom Ranch area only. See Researching Other Areas for more information.

Rim Camping

  • Backpackers who wish to stay above the rim entirely or include rim-top camping as part of a larger itinerary can do so on the North or South Rims. Options for Designated or At-Large backcountry camping exist. 


LIMITED AVAILABILITY

  • Demand for Grand Canyon backcountry permits often exceeds availability, and applicants are encouraged to apply early.
    • Lottery: Grand Canyon uses a monthly lottery to ensure fair consideration of earliest requests for Backcountry Permits (see Overview Tab for more information). 
    • Later Reservations: Sometimes space remains available after the Lottery month -- this space can be viewed and claimed through Recreation.gov.   
    • Watch for Cancellations: Space can also become available at later times due to cancellations, and cancellations are more likely to occur around 30-days before start dates (this is the last opportunity for permittees to cancel and receive partial refunds). Recreation.gov randomly releases this cancelled space online within 24-hours, and it tends to be claimed quickly. Recreation.gov allows new reservations as late as 5-days prior to the hike start date. 
    • Last Minute Waitlist: Grand Canyon holds back a very limited amount of space at Havasupai Gardens and Cottonwood Campground for in-park visitors seeking a last-minute permit. No last-minute space is held for Bright Angel Campground. These permits are issued in-person only at the Backcountry Information Center (BIC), are for one night, and cannot be purchased more than one day prior to the start of a hike:
      • Havasupai Gardens Waitlist Space is exclusively released at South Rim BIC: 
        • Jan 1 - Feb 29: 1 site for up to 6 people.
        • Mar 1 - Nov 30: 5 sites held for waitlist for up to 15 people.
        • Dec 1 - Dec 31: 1 site held for waitlist for 6 people.
      • Cottonwood Campground Waitlist Space is exclusively released at North Rim BIC:
        • May 15 - Oct 31: 1 site for up to 4 people. (No space held for remainder of year).
description.no_show_policy: No-shows are strongly frowned upon at Grand Canyon -- failing to cancel needlessly prevents other hikers from enjoying the canyon. If you know you can't make it, please take the time to cancel on recreation.gov right away.
description.quota_details:
Visitor Use Limits: The 1988 Backcountry Management Plan established use limits for each section ("use area") of the canyon. Use limits are described in terms of the total number of people as well as the number of small (1-6 person) and/or large (7-11 person) groups allowed in each area each night. Here are a few pertinent details:

  • Stay limits - All campgrounds and campsites have a stay limit of 2 nights per trip during the popular seasons. 
  • Affiliated Group Rule - No more than 1 permit from the same affiliated group (club, group of friends, etc.) can be in the same use area on the same night -- breaking this rule voids all permits.
  • Group Size - Limiting the size of your group to 6 or less will increase your chances of obtaining a permit as there are only a few large group sites.
  • Commercial Use - In addition to following all normal backcountry permit requirements, commercial organizations must obtain a Commercial Use Authorization.

Other Information / Frequently Asked Questions
description.season_information:
Plan When to Hike

  • Mar, Apr, and May: Weather fluctuates between ideal, extreme cold/snowstorms/icy trails, and inner-canyon heat exceeding 100 F in later May. Shoe traction devices may be necessary. 

  • Jun, Jul, and Aug: DANGEROUSLY hot! Temperatures in the bottom of the canyon can exceed 120 F (49 C). Even when hikers stop walking, not being able to get out of the sun and heat can be deadly. Rangers and experienced hikers recommend avoiding the canyon in the summer. 

  • Sep, Oct, and Nov: Summer heat and thunderstorms begin giving way to drier, more moderate temperatures with potential snow storms and icy trails late in the season. 

  • Dec, Jan, and Feb: Expect cold temperatures/snowy weather, but sunny days are more common. Trails will likely be icy at the top, and shoe traction devices may be necessary.

A remote drive-up camping site on the rim of the canyon.  

THRESHOLD Management Zone

There are two designated sites near the end of the road. The smaller sites for parties of 1-6 is on the east side of the road, while the larger sites for parties of 7-11 is on the west side, near the composting toilet. Camping is not permitted at the end of the road.

Plan on carrying all water for your time at Point Sublime and remember that campfires are not permitted in the backcountry of Grand Canyon National Park.

description_map.need_to_know:
There are two routes to reach this remote backcountry camping area. The recommend route begins at the Forest Service / NPS Boundary just south of USFS road 223. This route is generally passable for stock SUVs beginning in early to mid June after the snow has melted and the downed trees have been cleared for the season. If the road is blocked by downed trees, turn around, do not drive through the forest to get past the obstacles.

An alternate route begins near the Widforss Trailhead near the N.Rim developed area. This route is only recommended for folks with high-clearance 4WD vehicles. Though the distance might be shorter taking this route, the travel is much slower due to extremely poor road conditions. Road may be closed in early summer.
description_map.site_details: The W-1 Point Sublime road is currently closed to motorized vehicles. The only way to get to Point Sublime is by using roads coming in from the north. Camping at Point Sublime is designated 100 yards short of the final point on either side of the road near the toilet. The end of the road is day use only. Do not drive off-road or across meadows.  Hwy 67 and primitive road access to Sublime will close for the season by Nov 30 or earlier due to severe weather. Once roads are closed, they will remain closed until at least May 15. No services from Nov 1 through May 14. Especially in May but also at any time of the year there may be trees or other obstructions preventing passage on the difficult 4X4 access roads to this area

4675337032.description:
Bright Angel Campground is Grand Canyon’s premier hiking destination. Located at the bottom of the canyon, it has restrooms, potable water, shade trees, picnic tables, a Ranger Station, and proximity to Phantom Ranch Lodge. South Rim Hikers access via the South Kaibab Trail (7 miles and 4,840’ elev. change) or the Bright Angel Trail (9.5 miles and 4,440’ in elev. change). North Rim Hikers access via the North Kaibab Trail (14 miles and 5,820’ in elevation change). This area is appropriate for fit hikers who are ready for their first hike within the Grand Canyon backcountry.

Ranger programs are offered early March through November. Snacks and meals are available at the Phantom Ranch Lodge (meals must be reserved in advance 303-297-2757).

The campground has restrooms, potable water, shade trees, picnic tables, and a Ranger Station. This area is appropriate for breaking up the long hike out from Bright Angel Campground. This is for SHARED USE of the AZT large group site #33 at Bright Angel Campground. In April and May last minute permits are issued to up to 11 Arizona Trail Thru Hikers on multiple permits to share this site at Bright Angel Campground.

Bright Angel Campground is Grand Canyon’s premier hiking destination. Located at the bottom of the canyon, it has restrooms, potable water, shade trees, picnic tables, a Ranger Station, and proximity to Phantom Ranch Lodge. South Rim Hikers access via the South Kaibab Trail (7 miles and 4,840’ elev. change) or the Bright Angel Trail (9.5 miles and 4,440’ in elev. change). North Rim Hikers access via the North Kaibab Trail (14 miles and 5,820’ in elevation change).

Potable drinking water is available seasonally (mid-May to mid-Oct) at the campground. During other times of the year be prepared to filter/treat water obtained from the creek. There are deer, ringtail cats, and squirrels in the area. Day hike destinations include Roaring Springs, Manzanita Canyon, and the North Rim.

4675337044.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: One of the more difficult south-side trails for hikers with extensive Grand Canyon experience. Due to a complete lack of shade and water, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September.

Primitive Management Zone

Established campsites are found at the 75-Mile Canyon Saddle, above and below the Redwall Limestone, and at the Colorado River. There is a composting toilet just upriver from the mouth of Tanner Canyon (bring your own toilet paper).

description_map.need_to_know:
Trail Description:

  • Tanner Trail  

Distances: 

  • Lipan Point to Colorado River: 9 miles (-4700’)

The Tanner Trail is completely dry. If caching water for your hike out, be sure to place it out of sight and label it with your name and pick-up date. Do not abandon unused caches.

Lipan Point Road will be CLOSED June 22 to December 23, 2026. Tanner Trail users must park their vehicles at "No Name Point," approximately 1,000 feet west of Lipan Point Road on Highway 64 and walk to the Tanner Trailhead. Use caution when walking along Highway 64.
description_map.site_details: Lipan Point Road will be CLOSED June 22 to December 23, 2026. Tanner Trail users must park their vehicles at "No Name Point," approximately 1,000 feet west of Lipan Point Road on Highway 64 and walk to the Tanner Trailhead. Use caution when walking along Highway 64. Due to intense heat and the lack of shade and water along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. Date your water caches and remove them when leaving. Dunes on both sides of Tanner Drainage are closed to visitation. Toilets are located 300' east of rapids (do NOT throw trash in toilet). Urinate in the river, not on beaches or on vegetation. No Fires.

4675337044.district: Requires Adv GC Experience or Unusual

4675337045.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: The New Hance Trail is one of the more difficult trails for hikers with extensive experience at Grand Canyon. Due to the lack of shade and reliable water, it is not recommended to hike here late May through mid-September. Route finding skills are necessary on some sections of trail.

Primitive Management Zone

Good campsites can be found above and below the Redwall, in the bed of Red Canyon, and downstream of Hance Rapids. Though there are nice sites above the rapids, these sites are regularly used by river trips who will not have the flexibility to continue downriver. If a river trip shows up, they will likely ask you to move or share the camp with you. Only choose these sites if you arrive late.

description_map.need_to_know:

  • New Hance Trail  

Distances:

  • Trailhead to bed of Red Canyon: 4.9 miles
  • Bed of Red Canyon to Colorado River: 1.6 miles

Seasonal water may be found where the trail first reaches the bed of Red Canyon.
description_map.site_details: Due to intense heat and the lack of shade and water along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. New Hance trail parking is a half mile west of trailhead on south side spur road. Bury human waste in soil at least 200 feet from river and camps but never in sand dunes. Pack out all toilet paper. Urinate in the river, not on beaches or on vegetation. Appropriate human waste disposal areas are limited, consider a carry out method, dispose in trash can after exiting canyon. Beach areas are shared with river trips. No Fires.

4675337045.district: Requires Adv GC Experience or Unusual

4675337046.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: The Escalante Route is for hikers with extensive overnight backpacking experience at Grand Canyon. This trail is accessed from the Tanner Trail, the New Hance Trail, or the Tonto Trail. It is not recommended on the first or last night of an itinerary. Due to the lack of shade, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. There are several challenges along this route which are spelled out in the trail description.

Primitive Management Zone

Good beach camps can be found at Cardenas Creek, Escalante Creek, Seventyfive Mile Creek, and Papago Creek. These beaches are often used by river trips so plan on sharing your space with large river trips.

description_map.need_to_know:
Trail Description:

  • Escalante Route  

Distances:

  • Tanner Beach to Cardenas Creek: 3 miles

  • Cardenas Creek to Seventyfive Mile Creek: 7 miles

  • Seventyfive Mile Creek to Hance Rapids: 2 miles

The Colorado River is the only source of water along this route.

Lipan Point Road will be CLOSED June 22 to December 23, 2026. Tanner Trail users must park their vehicles at "No Name Point," approximately 1,000 feet west of Lipan Point Road on Highway 64 and walk to the Tanner Trailhead. Use caution when walking along Highway 64.
description_map.site_details: Lipan Point Rd CLOSED 6/22-12/23/26. Tanner Trail users must park at No Name Point, 1000ft W of Lipan Point Rd and walk to trailhead. Use caution walking along Hwy 64. This hike is NOT recommended late May to mid-Sept due to intense heat, no shade, & no water. Do not bury human waste in sand; bury it in soil at least 200ft from river & camps. Pack out toilet paper. Urinate in the river, not on beaches or vegetation. Share beaches with river trips. No fires. At Cardenas, do not walk on sand dunes above main river camps. Avoid using trails that appear to have been rehabilitated. There is a habitat restoration site at Cardenas with trees that need watering. Interested in helping? Learn more: https://www.nps.gov/grca/learn/nature/cardenas.htm

4675337047.description:

Due to the lack of shade and water, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. The trail between Horseshoe Mesa and Hance Creek may not be suitable for those with a fear of heights due to rough, washed out, and exposed sections.

Primitive Management Zone

Established campsites can be found where the trail crosses the Hance Creek drainage.

  • Grandview Trailhead to Horseshoe Mesa (BF5): 3 miles
  • Horseshoe Mesa to Hance Creek: 1.9 miles
  • Hance Creek to Hance Rapids (BD9): 6.5 miles

Perennial water can be found at Page Springs and Hance Creek.
description_map.site_details: Due to intense heat and the lack of shade and water along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. Urinate at least 200 feet away from creek and camp. Water Warning: Water at Page/Miners Spring may exceed EPA MUNICIPAL drinking water standards for arsenic. Keep in mind the dehydration threats from not drinking can be much more immediate and life threatening.

4675337048.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: This use-area is for hikers who have extensive overnight backpacking experience at Grand Canyon. This is one of the most difficult trails on the south side of the canyon. The descent through the Supai Formation is heavily damaged due to rockfall. The Redwall descent is steep and exposed. Due to the lack of shade along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September.

Primitive Management Zone

Well established dry camps can be found below Yuma point atop a slickrock outctropping. Another dry camp can be found near White’s Butte. There are several nice sites found next to Boucher Creek and on the beach next to the Colorado River.

4675337049.description:

This trail is accessed from the Tanner Trail and is not recommended on the first or last night of an itinerary. Due to the lack of shade and water, it is not recommended to camp here from late May through mid-September. Some portions of this trail are narrow and exposed and might not be suitable for those with a fear of heights.

Primitive Management Zone

There are multiple established campsites between Comanche Creek and Palisades Creek. Beyond Palisades Creek, camping is quite limited until reaching a small beach ½ mile downriver from the confluence with the Little Colorado River (LCR).

North of Little Colorado River:

  • Navajo Nation permits are also required if you plan on accessing this area from the rim anywhere North of the Little Colorado River.

Lipan Point Road will be CLOSED June 22 to December 23, 2026. Tanner Trail users must park their vehicles at "No Name Point," approximately 1,000 feet west of Lipan Point Road on Highway 64 and walk to the Tanner Trailhead. Use caution when walking along Highway 64.
description_map.site_details: Lipan Point Rd CLOSED 6/22-12/23/26. Tanner Trail users must park at No Name Point, 1000ft W of Lipan Point Rd and walk to the trailhead. Salt Mines are off limits and closed to visitation! Water from the LCR is not potable. To protect endangered fish habitat: stream crossings are only allowed 0.2 miles upstream of confluence, no launching or landing boats in the LCR channel. Mar 1 through Nov 30: no swimming or wading allowed in southern half of LCR. Navajo Nation permits are required if accessing the area from the rim anywhere North of the LCR.

4675337050.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: This use-area is for hikers who have extensive backpacking experience at Grand Canyon. Due to the lack of shade and reliable water, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. There is a 20’ rappel that requires basic canyoneering skills (ACA rating: 3A VI). This may be the most challenging route on the south side of Grand Canyon. A portion of the road leading to this remote trailhead is closed requiring an additional 7 miles of walking from Forest Service Road 328 at the Havasupai Reservation Boundary.

Primitive Management Zone

Established campsites can be found atop the Esplanade, in the Royal Arch Drainage, Toltec Beach, Copper Canyon, and along the South Bass Trail

  • Boucher Trail to South Bass Trail

  • Esplanade Junction to Royal Arch: 12.6 miles
  • Royal Arch to Toltec Beach: 3 miles
  • Toltec Beach to Copper Canyon: 9 miles
  • Copper Canyon to Bass Canyon: 3.3 miles
  • Bass Canyon to South Bass Trailhead: 4.3 miles

Water Status: 

Perennial water sources include Royal Arch Canyon (Redwall gorge) and at the Colorado River. Seasonal water (during cooler weather or just after rains) is sometimes available from Seep Spring (between Chemehuevi and Toltec Points), in Copper Canyon, and from potholes in Bass Canyon (below the Tonto Trail crossing). Garnet Canyon is extremely mineralized and is considered undrinkable.
description_map.site_details: Due to intense heat and the lack of shade and water along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. Royal Arch Loop includes 20' rappel! Do not leave fixed lines at rappel. No camping within 1/4 mile of Elves Chasm or Royal Arch Creek. Due to Havasupai Reservation closure, parking is 7-miles away from South Bass Trailhead, along FR328 near the Havasupai Reservation boundary. For details, see Access Map for South Bass Trailhead. Cryptobiotic soil is a living crust that prevents erosion and helps desert plants get water. 'Don't bust the crust!' Stay on the trails. No Fires.

4675337083.description:
The North Rim Horse Camp is located on CC Hill. To access the site, drive a short, gated dirt road north of the North Kaibab Trailhead. This road also provides access to the concessionaire mule barns, a volunteer camping area, and an open air storage area for the NPS. Vehicles accessing the site must yield passage to the concessionaire mules when mules are present on the roadway.

The North Rim Horse Camp consists of a small corral, a picnic table, and a parking area. The corral measures 35’ by 45’ and was built for six equines. The corral has a trough and water spigot. The parking area is shared with the volunteer camping area. The parking area is 40’ wide at its widest spot (delineated by large logs) and is approximately 160’ long.

description_map.need_to_know:
Group Size: Total group size (above) must include the total people plus stock staying in this site. Within this number, cannot exceed 6 people nor 6 stock.

Prohibited: Llamas, goats, and other non-equine stock.

Health: Must carry a negative Coggins test certificate for each equine.

Vehicles: Limited to no more than 2 vehicles plus 2 tow vehicles (30' in length or less) and only for the nights listed in this site. There is a separate designated parking area for nights when stock users are traveling through the canyon.

Removal and Cleanup: Permittee is responsible for manure clean-up, pet excrement disposal, and removal of dead or injured animals.

See Stock Use Handout for more information.
description_map.site_details: CHECKIN: Private stock users MUST check-in at the Backcountry Information Center between noon and 5pm, prior to occupying the site. Be ready to show a required negative Coggins result for each equine, the signed permit, and the Private Stock Use Handout (read handout for other important requirments). Quiet hours: 10pm-6am. Generator hours: 7-9am and 6-8pm. Check-out MUST be by 11am (office opens at 8am). Before leaving, bring all manure from the site and dump it in the dumpster by the backcountry office. Note that others may also be camping in an Admin camp nearby. Total group size (above) must include people plus stock. Limit of 2 vehicles plus 2 tow vehicles (30' in length or less) and only for the nights listed in this site.

4675337107.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: One of the more difficult south-side trails for hikers with extensive Grand Canyon experience. Due to a complete lack of shade and water, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September.

Primitive Management Zone

Established campsites are found at the 75-Mile Canyon Saddle, above and below the Redwall Limestone, and at the Colorado River. There is a composting toilet just upriver from the mouth of Tanner Canyon (bring your own toilet paper).

Lipan Point Road will be CLOSED June 22 to December 23, 2026. Tanner Trail users must park their vehicles at "No Name Point," approximately 1,000 feet west of Lipan Point Road on Highway 64 and walk to the Tanner Trailhead. Use caution when walking along Highway 64.

4675337108.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: The New Hance Trail is one of the more difficult trails for hikers with extensive experience at Grand Canyon. Due to the lack of shade and reliable water, it is not recommended to hike here late May through mid-September. Route finding skills are necessary on some sections of trail.

Primitive Management Zone

Good campsites can be found above and below the Redwall, in the bed of Red Canyon, and downstream of Hance Rapids. Though there are nice sites above the rapids, these sites are regularly used by river trips who will not have the flexibility to continue downriver. If a river trip shows up, they will likely ask you to move or share the camp with you. Only choose these sites if you arrive late.

4675337109.description:
Requires Advanced Grand Canyon Experience: The Escalante Route is for hikers with extensive overnight backpacking experience at Grand Canyon. This trail is accessed from the Tanner Trail, the New Hance Trail, or the Tonto Trail. It is not recommended on the first or last night of an itinerary. Due to the lack of shade, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. There are several challenges along this route which are spelled out in the trail description.

Primitive Management Zone

Good beach camps can be found at Cardenas Creek, Escalante Creek, Seventyfive Mile Creek, and Papago Creek. These beaches are often used by river trips so plan on sharing your space with large river trips.

This is one of the most difficult trails on the south side of the canyon. The descent through the Supai Formation is heavily damaged due to rockfall. The Redwall descent is steep and exposed. Due to the lack of shade along the trail, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September.

Primitive Management Zone

Well established dry camps can be found below Yuma point atop a slickrock outctropping. Another dry camp can be found near White’s Butte. There are several nice sites found next to Boucher Creek and on the beach next to the Colorado River.

Some portions of this trail are narrow and exposed and might not be suitable for those with a fear of heights.

Due to the lack of shade and reliable water, it is not recommended to hike here from late May through mid-September. There is a 20’ rappel that requires basic canyoneering skills (ACA rating: 3A VI). This may be the most challenging route on the south side of Grand Canyon. A portion of the road leading to this remote trailhead is closed requiring an additional 7 miles of walking from Forest Service Road 328 at the Havasupai Reservation Boundary.

Primitive Management Zone

Established campsites can be found atop the Esplanade, in the Royal Arch Drainage, Toltec Beach, Copper Canyon, and along the South Bass Trail

Garnet Canyon is extremely mineralized and is considered undrinkable.

Due to Havasupai Reservation closure, parking is 7-miles away from South Bass Trailhead, along FR328 near the Havasupai Reservation boundary. For details, see Access Map for South Bass Trailhead. Cryptobiotic soil is a living crust that prevents erosion and helps desert plants get water. 'Don't bust the crust!' Stay on the trails. Due to the lack of shade and water, it is not recommended to camp here late May through mid-September.

Primitive Management Zone

Several well-established slickrock campsites can be found throughout the area, including a few overhang camps halfway between the Bill Hall / Thunder River Trail junction and the lip of Surprise Valley. Be sure to avoid trampling the cryptobiotic soil crusts when travelling to and from campsites.

4675337167.description:
Description: Cottonwood Campground is located about mid-way between the North Rim and Bright Angel Campground. The campground has an emergency phone and toilets. This area is essential for breaking up the long and difficult 14-mile hike between Bright Angel Campground and the North Rim. 

Potable drinking water is available seasonally (mid-May to mid-Oct) at the campground. During other times of the year be prepared to filter/treat water obtained from the creek. There are deer, ringtail cats, and squirrels in the area. Day hike destinations include Roaring Springs, Manzanita Canyon, and the North Rim.  

Winter Season Warning: All North Rim roads and services are closed for the winter from Dec 1 through May 14th.

4675337171.description: Primitive Management Zone. Bring all water needed for the duration of the permit. Springs found on a map can not be relied upon. Watch out for bison wandering free in this zone. Campfires are prohibited in the backcountry. Camps must be out of site of any paved road. The Arizona Trail passes through this zone. It is a flat, easy to follow trail in this zone.

description_map.need_to_know: Especially in May but also at any time of the year there may be trees or other obstructions preventing passage on the difficult 4X4 access roads to this area. No Camping is allowed along Hwy 67. Camping in the meadow known as The Basin and up to 100 feet within the trees around the meadow is not allowed. The W-1 Point Sublime road is a very difficult four wheel drive road where a lifted vehicle with proper self rescue equipment is highly recommended. There are very few 4X4 camping spots along Point Sublime road. Vehicles must be kept on the road at all times. This zone ends one mile east of the W-1/W-4 junction on the W-1 road. Camping on the last mile of the W-1 Point Sublime road is not allowed.

description_map.site_details: River Assisted Backcountry Travel (RABT) is Authorized on this Permit with conditions: 1) RABT travel must be solely for crossing the river to access a route or trail on the other side or to a nearby route or trail. 2) A Type III or Type V PFD must be worn by each person while on the water. 3) Total travel on river is limited to 8 miles. 4) Any packraft or device used on the river for RABT must be carried in and out by the person. 5) RABT use may not occur between Lees Ferry (RM 0) and the Navajo Bridge (RM 4.5) or between Boat Beach (RM 88) and Pipe Creek (RM 89.5). 6) All equipment must be Cleaned, Drained, and Dried between waterways to avoid spread of invasive species. 7) Camp away from river corridor or in very small river camps.

4675337175.description:
Bright Angel Campground is Grand Canyon’s premier hiking destination. Located at the bottom of the canyon, it has restrooms, potable water, shade trees, picnic tables, a Ranger Station, and proximity to Phantom Ranch Lodge. South Rim Hikers access via the South Kaibab Trail (7 miles and 4,840’ elev. change) or the Bright Angel Trail (9.5 miles and 4,440’ in elev. change). North Rim Hikers access via the North Kaibab Trail (14 miles and 5,820’ in elevation change). This area is appropriate for fit hikers who are ready for their first hike within the Grand Canyon backcountry.

Ranger programs are offered early March through November. Snacks and meals are available at the Phantom Ranch Lodge (meals must be reserved in advance 303-297-2757).

4675337178.description: HEAT WARNING: Please rethink your hike! Hiking in the desert of Grand Canyon within the hottest time of the year carries inherent risk -- this is the time when experienced Grand Canyon Hikers typically avoid the canyon. At the bottom, summer temperatures can reach 120, and there is little to no shade. To survive, avoid hiking between 10am and 4pm. Please see www.nps.gov/grca/planyourvisit/hike-smart.htm for hiking tips to help you and your group understand the risks and prepare.
